claim: Viral inclusion bodies (IBs) commonly form during the replication of Ebola virus (EBOV) in infected cells.
source: Viral inclusion bodies (IBs) commonly form during the replication of Ebola virus (EBOV) in infected cells, but their role in viral immune evasion has rarely been explored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about EBOV replication.

claim: The role of viral inclusion bodies in viral immune evasion has rarely been explored.
source: Viral inclusion bodies (IBs) commonly form during the replication of Ebola virus (EBOV) in infected cells, but their role in viral immune evasion has rarely been explored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: IRF3, but not TBK1 or IKKε, was recruited and sequestered in viral IBs when cells were infected by EBOV trVLPs.
source: Here, we found that interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), but not TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) or IκB kinase epsilon (IKKε), was recruited and sequestered in viral IBs when the cells were infected by EBOV transcription- and replication-competent virus-like particles (trVLPs).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1A-F demonstrating IRF3 colocalization with VP35 in IBs, while TBK1 and IKKε do not colocalize.

claim: Nucleoprotein/virion protein 35 (VP35)-induced IBs formation was critical for IRF3 recruitment and sequestration.
source: Nucleoprotein/virion protein 35 (VP35)-induced IBs formation was critical for IRF3 recruitment and sequestration, probably through interaction with STING.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing that coexpression of NP and VP35 results in substantial sequestration of IRF3 in IB-like structures.

claim: VP35-induced IBs formation probably occurs through interaction with STING.
source: Nucleoprotein/virion protein 35 (VP35)-induced IBs formation was critical for IRF3 recruitment and sequestration, probably through interaction with STING.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing VP35 interacts with STING and STING is recruited to IBs, and STING knockdown reduces IRF3 sequestration.

claim: The association of TBK1 and IRF3 was blocked by EBOV trVLPs infection.
source: Consequently, the association of TBK1 and IRF3, which plays a vital role in type I interferon (IFN-I) induction, was blocked by EBOV trVLPs infection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assay data in Figure 3A-B showing reduced TBK1-IRF3 complexes in trVLP-infected cells, and immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3C.

claim: IRF3 phosphorylation induced by Sendai virus or poly(I:C) stimulation was suppressed by EBOV trVLPs.
source: Additionally, IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation induced by Sendai virus or poly(I:C) stimulation were suppressed by EBOV trVLPs.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3D showing reduced IRF3 phosphorylation, and immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A-B showing reduced nuclear translocation.

claim: IRF3 nuclear translocation induced by Sendai virus or poly(I:C) stimulation was suppressed by EBOV trVLPs.
source: Additionally, IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation induced by Sendai virus or poly(I:C) stimulation were suppressed by EBOV trVLPs.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A-B showing reduced nuclear IRF3 distribution in trVLP-infected cells.

claim: Downregulation of STING significantly attenuated VP35-induced IRF3 accumulation in IBs.
source: Furthermore, downregulation of STING significantly attenuated VP35-induced IRF3 accumulation in IBs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6F-G showing reduced IRF3 sequestration in IBs when STING is knocked down by siRNA.

claim: Coexpression of viral proteins by which IB-like structures formed was much more potent in antagonizing IFN-I than expression of VP35 alone.
source: Coexpression of the viral proteins by which IB-like structures formed was much more potent in antagonizing IFN-I than expression of the IFN-I antagonist VP35 alone.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 7B showing greater suppression of IFN-β-Luc expression with NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression compared to VP35 alone.

claim: EBOV uses a novel immune evasion mechanism to evade host innate immunity.
source: These results suggested a novel immune evasion mechanism by which EBOV evades host innate immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ebola virus disease is the deadliest infectious disease caused by infection with EBOV.
source: Ebola virus (EBOV) disease is the deadliest infectious disease caused by infection with EBOV, an enveloped, nonsegmented negative-sense RNA virus (Feldmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feldmann et al., 2003.

claim: EBOV is an enveloped, nonsegmented negative-sense RNA virus.
source: Ebola virus (EBOV) disease is the deadliest infectious disease caused by infection with EBOV, an enveloped, nonsegmented negative-sense RNA virus (Feldmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feldmann et al., 2003.

claim: The EBOV genome is 19 kb.
source: The 19 kb viral genome comprises seven genes encoding the nucleoprotein (NP), virion protein 35 (VP35), VP40, glycoprotein (GP), VP30, VP24, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L) (Mahanty and Bray, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mahanty and Bray, 2004.

claim: The EBOV genome comprises seven genes encoding NP, VP35, VP40, GP, VP30, VP24, and L.
source: The 19 kb viral genome comprises seven genes encoding the nucleoprotein (NP), virion protein 35 (VP35), VP40, glycoprotein (GP), VP30, VP24, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L) (Mahanty and Bray, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mahanty and Bray, 2004.

claim: Inclusion bodies that form in EBOV-infected cells are specialized intracellular compartments that serve as sites for EBOV replication and the generation of progeny viral RNPs.
source: Inclusion bodies (IBs) that form in EBOV-infected cells are specialized intracellular compartments that serve as sites for EBOV replication and the generation of progeny viral RNPs (Hoenen et al., 2012; Nanbo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hoenen et al., 2012 and Nanbo et al., 2013.

claim: In IBs, the EBOV genome is replicated and transcribed by viral polymerase complexes.
source: In IBs, the EBOV genome is replicated and transcribed by viral polymerase complexes (Misasi and Sullivan, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Misasi and Sullivan, 2014.

claim: VP35 serves as a cofactor of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
source: VP35 serves as a cofactor of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and contributes to viral replication by homo-oligomerization through a coiled-coil domain (Reid et al., 2005) as well as through its phosphorylation and ubiquitination, which was recently discovered (van Tol et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reid et al., 2005, van Tol et al., 2022, and Zhu et al., 2020.

claim: VP35 contributes to viral replication by homo-oligomerization through a coiled-coil domain.
source: VP35 serves as a cofactor of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and contributes to viral replication by homo-oligomerization through a coiled-coil domain (Reid et al., 2005) as well as through its phosphorylation and ubiquitination, which was recently discovered (van Tol et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reid et al., 2005.

claim: VP35 contributes to viral replication through its phosphorylation and ubiquitination.
source: VP35 serves as a cofactor of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and contributes to viral replication by homo-oligomerization through a coiled-coil domain (Reid et al., 2005) as well as through its phosphorylation and ubiquitination, which was recently discovered (van Tol et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Tol et al., 2022 and Zhu et al., 2020.

claim: Innate interferon responses constitute the first lines of host defense against viral infection.
source: Innate interferon responses constitute the first lines of host defense against viral infection.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about innate immunity.

claim: RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), including RIG-I and melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5, play pivotal roles in the response to RNA virus infection.
source: Retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors (RLRs), including RIG-I and melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5, play pivotal roles in the response to RNA virus infection.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about innate immunity.

claim: After recognition of RNA virus infection, RIG-I is recruited to MAVS through the caspase activation and recruitment domain.
source: After the recognition of RNA virus infection, RIG-I is recruited to the mitochondrial antiviral adaptor protein (MAVS) through the caspase activation and recruitment domain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the RIG-I signaling pathway.

claim: The activation of MAVS recruits multiple downstream signaling components to mitochondria, leading to the activation of IKKε and TBK1.
source: The activation of MAVS recruits multiple downstream signaling components to mitochondria, leading to the activation of inhibitor of κ-B kinase ε (IKKε) and TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), which in turn phosphorylate IFN regulatory factor 3 (IRF3).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the RIG-I signaling pathway.

claim: IKKε and TBK1 phosphorylate IRF3.
source: The activation of MAVS recruits multiple downstream signaling components to mitochondria, leading to the activation of inhibitor of κ-B kinase ε (IKKε) and TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), which in turn phosphorylate IFN regulatory factor 3 (IRF3).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the RIG-I signaling pathway.

claim: Phosphorylated IRF3 forms a dimer that translocates to the nucleus.
source: Phosphorylated IRF3 forms a dimer that translocates to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of type I interferon (IFN-I) genes (Fitzgerald et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fitzgerald et al., 2003 and Liu et al., 2015.

claim: Phosphorylated IRF3 dimers activate the transcription of type I interferon genes in the nucleus.
source: Phosphorylated IRF3 forms a dimer that translocates to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of type I interferon (IFN-I) genes (Fitzgerald et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fitzgerald et al., 2003 and Liu et al., 2015.

claim: Viruses have evolved various strategies to evade or subvert host antiviral responses to promote viral replication and persistence.
source: To promote viral replication and persistence, viruses have evolved various strategies to evade or subvert host antiviral responses.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about viral immune evasion.

claim: SFTSV has developed a mechanism to evade host immune responses through the interaction between nonstructural proteins and IFN-I induction proteins, including TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7.
source: For example, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) has developed a mechanism to evade host immune responses through the interaction between nonstructural proteins and IFN-I induction proteins, including TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7 (Hong et al., 2019; Lee and Shin, 2021; Ning et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014), sequestering them inside SFTSV-induced cytoplasmic structures known as IBs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2019; Lee and Shin, 2021; Ning et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014.

claim: SFTSV sequesters TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7 inside SFTSV-induced cytoplasmic structures known as IBs.
source: For example, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) has developed a mechanism to evade host immune responses through the interaction between nonstructural proteins and IFN-I induction proteins, including TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7 (Hong et al., 2019; Lee and Shin, 2021; Ning et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014), sequestering them inside SFTSV-induced cytoplasmic structures known as IBs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2019; Lee and Shin, 2021; Ning et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014.

claim: SFTSV nonstructural proteins can hijack STAT1 and STAT2 in IBs to suppress IFN-I signaling.
source: In addition to inhibiting IFN-I induction, SFTSV nonstructural proteins can hijack STAT1 and STAT2 in IBs to suppress IFN-I signaling (Ning et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ning et al., 2015.

claim: Viral IBs can act as virus-built 'jails' that sequester crucial host factors and interfere with corresponding cellular processes.
source: These studies highlight the role of viral IBs as virus-built 'jails' that sequester some crucial host factors and interfere with the corresponding cellular processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited SFTSV studies.

claim: EBOV uses various approaches to evade the host immune response, including antagonizing IFN production, inhibiting IFN signaling, and enhancing IFN resistance.
source: EBOV uses various approaches to evade the host immune response, including antagonizing IFN production, inhibiting IFN signaling, and enhancing IFN resistance (Basler et al., 2000; McCarthy et al., 2016; Reid et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basler et al., 2000; McCarthy et al., 2016; Reid et al., 2006.

claim: VP35 is an IFN-I inhibitor that antagonizes host innate immunity by interacting with TBK1 and IKKε.
source: VP35 is an IFN-I inhibitor that antagonizes host innate immunity by interacting with TBK1 and IKKε (Basler et al., 2003; Prins et al., 2009), suppressing RNA silencing and inhibiting dendritic cell maturation (Haasnoot et al., 2007; Yen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basler et al., 2003 and Prins et al., 2009.

claim: VP35 antagonizes host innate immunity by suppressing RNA silencing.
source: VP35 is an IFN-I inhibitor that antagonizes host innate immunity by interacting with TBK1 and IKKε (Basler et al., 2003; Prins et al., 2009), suppressing RNA silencing and inhibiting dendritic cell maturation (Haasnoot et al., 2007; Yen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haasnoot et al., 2007.

claim: VP35 antagonizes host innate immunity by inhibiting dendritic cell maturation.
source: VP35 is an IFN-I inhibitor that antagonizes host innate immunity by interacting with TBK1 and IKKε (Basler et al., 2003; Prins et al., 2009), suppressing RNA silencing and inhibiting dendritic cell maturation (Haasnoot et al., 2007; Yen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yen et al., 2014.

claim: Viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells play a role in immune evasion by sequestering IRF3 into IBs and preventing the interaction of IRF3 with TBK1 and IKKε.
source: Here, we report that viral IBs in EBOV transcription- and replication-competent virus-like particle (trVLP)-infected cells appear to play a role in immune evasion by sequestering IRF3 into IBs and preventing the interaction of IRF3 with TBK1 and IKKε.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: IBs with a unique structure and viral particles formed in the cytoplasm when HepG2 cells were infected with EBOV trVLPs.
source: When HepG2 cells were infected with EBOV trVLPs (Hoenen et al., 2014), which authentically model the complete virus life cycle, IBs with a unique structure and viral particles formed in the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transmission electron microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing IBs and viral particles.

claim: EBOV trVLPs authentically model the complete virus life cycle.
source: When HepG2 cells were infected with EBOV trVLPs (Hoenen et al., 2014), which authentically model the complete virus life cycle, IBs with a unique structure and viral particles formed in the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoenen et al., 2014.

claim: A substantial percentage of endogenous IRF3 was trapped in viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells with large IBs.
source: Surprisingly, we found that a substantial percentage of endogenous IRF3 was trapped in viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells with large IBs (Figure 1A, B), while no detectable TBK1 or IKKε, the essential upstream components of IRF3 signaling (Fitzgerald et al., 2003), was sequestered in the viral IBs (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 1A, B showing IRF3 colocalization with VP35 in IBs.

claim: No detectable TBK1 was sequestered in viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that a substantial percentage of endogenous IRF3 was trapped in viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells with large IBs (Figure 1A, B), while no detectable TBK1 or IKKε, the essential upstream components of IRF3 signaling (Fitzgerald et al., 2003), was sequestered in the viral IBs (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 1C, D showing no colocalization of TBK1 with VP35 in IBs.

claim: No detectable IKKε was sequestered in viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that a substantial percentage of endogenous IRF3 was trapped in viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells with large IBs (Figure 1A, B), while no detectable TBK1 or IKKε, the essential upstream components of IRF3 signaling (Fitzgerald et al., 2003), was sequestered in the viral IBs (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 1E, F showing no colocalization of IKKε with VP35 in IBs.

claim: TBK1 and IKKε are essential upstream components of IRF3 signaling.
source: Surprisingly, we found that a substantial percentage of endogenous IRF3 was trapped in viral IBs in EBOV trVLP-infected cells with large IBs (Figure 1A, B), while no detectable TBK1 or IKKε, the essential upstream components of IRF3 signaling (Fitzgerald et al., 2003), was sequestered in the viral IBs (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fitzgerald et al., 2003.

claim: IRF3 was specifically compartmentalized in viral IBs.
source: These results suggested that IRF3 was specifically compartmentalized in viral IBs, and this compartmentalization spatially isolated IRF3 from its upstream activators TBK1 and IKKε.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that IRF3, but not TBK1 or IKKε, colocalizes with IBs.

claim: The compartmentalization of IRF3 in viral IBs spatially isolated IRF3 from its upstream activators TBK1 and IKKε.
source: These results suggested that IRF3 was specifically compartmentalized in viral IBs, and this compartmentalization spatially isolated IRF3 from its upstream activators TBK1 and IKKε.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that IRF3 is in IBs while TBK1 and IKKε are not.

claim: Detectable IRF3 puncta colocalized with viral proteins were apparent at 36 hpi in infected cells.
source: Detectable IRF3 puncta colocalized with viral proteins were apparent at 36 hpi in infected cells and correlated significantly with the size and shape of the viral IBs (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 2A showing IRF3 puncta at 36 hpi.

claim: IRF3 puncta correlated significantly with the size and shape of viral IBs.
source: Detectable IRF3 puncta colocalized with viral proteins were apparent at 36 hpi in infected cells and correlated significantly with the size and shape of the viral IBs (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis in Figure 2B showing increasing IRF3 distribution in IBs over time.

claim: Nearly all IRF3 colocalized with viral IBs at 48 hpi.
source: As the size of IBs increased at 48 hpi, nearly all IRF3 colocalized with viral IBs, whereas the IRF3 distribution was completely different in the uninfected cells nearby (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 2A and quantitative analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: The intensity of the IRF3 signal in the puncta increased as the level of cytoplasmic-dispersed IRF3 decreased as infection proceeded.
source: As infection proceeded, the intensity of the IRF3 signal in the puncta increased as the level of cytoplasmic-dispersed IRF3 decreased (Figure 2A), indicating that the total amount of IRF3 in the cells did not dramatically change during infection (Figure 2D, E) and that only its subcellular localization changed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 2A showing redistribution of IRF3 over time.

claim: The total amount of IRF3 in cells did not dramatically change during EBOV trVLP infection.
source: As infection proceeded, the intensity of the IRF3 signal in the puncta increased as the level of cytoplasmic-dispersed IRF3 decreased (Figure 2A), indicating that the total amount of IRF3 in the cells did not dramatically change during infection (Figure 2D, E) and that only its subcellular localization changed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting in Figure 2D and quantitative analysis in Figure 2E showing no significant change in total IRF3 levels.

claim: Only the subcellular localization of IRF3 changed during EBOV trVLP infection.
source: As infection proceeded, the intensity of the IRF3 signal in the puncta increased as the level of cytoplasmic-dispersed IRF3 decreased (Figure 2A), indicating that the total amount of IRF3 in the cells did not dramatically change during infection (Figure 2D, E) and that only its subcellular localization changed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that total IRF3 levels remain constant while its distribution changes.

claim: IRF3 is a critical transcription factor in the IFN induction pathway.
source: Upon virus infection, IRF3, as a critical transcription factor in the IFN induction pathway, can be phosphorylated and activated by TBK1, and then phosphorylated IRF3 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus, eliciting the expression of antiviral IFNs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the IFN induction pathway.

claim: IRF3 can be phosphorylated and activated by TBK1 upon virus infection.
source: Upon virus infection, IRF3, as a critical transcription factor in the IFN induction pathway, can be phosphorylated and activated by TBK1, and then phosphorylated IRF3 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus, eliciting the expression of antiviral IFNs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the IFN induction pathway.

claim: Phosphorylated IRF3 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus.
source: Upon virus infection, IRF3, as a critical transcription factor in the IFN induction pathway, can be phosphorylated and activated by TBK1, and then phosphorylated IRF3 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus, eliciting the expression of antiviral IFNs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the IFN induction pathway.

claim: Phosphorylated IRF3 in the nucleus elicits the expression of antiviral IFNs.
source: Upon virus infection, IRF3, as a critical transcription factor in the IFN induction pathway, can be phosphorylated and activated by TBK1, and then phosphorylated IRF3 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus, eliciting the expression of antiviral IFNs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the IFN induction pathway.

claim: Cytoplasmic complexes consisting of endogenous TBK1 with IRF3 were observed in HepG2 cells treated with poly(I:C).
source: Cytoplasmic complexes consisting of endogenous TBK1 with IRF3 (the red signal) were observed in HepG2 cells treated with poly(I:C), which induces the activation of the RIG-I signal cascade and IRF3 phosphorylation, and poly(I:C)-induced TBK1:IRF3 complexes were significantly reduced by EBOV trVLPs infection (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assay in Figure 3A showing red signals representing TBK1-IRF3 complexes.

claim: Poly(I:C) induces the activation of the RIG-I signal cascade and IRF3 phosphorylation.
source: Cytoplasmic complexes consisting of endogenous TBK1 with IRF3 (the red signal) were observed in HepG2 cells treated with poly(I:C), which induces the activation of the RIG-I signal cascade and IRF3 phosphorylation, and poly(I:C)-induced TBK1:IRF3 complexes were significantly reduced by EBOV trVLPs infection (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about poly(I:C) as a RIG-I agonist.

claim: Poly(I:C)-induced TBK1:IRF3 complexes were significantly reduced by EBOV trVLPs infection.
source: Cytoplasmic complexes consisting of endogenous TBK1 with IRF3 (the red signal) were observed in HepG2 cells treated with poly(I:C), which induces the activation of the RIG-I signal cascade and IRF3 phosphorylation, and poly(I:C)-induced TBK1:IRF3 complexes were significantly reduced by EBOV trVLPs infection (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assay in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3B showing reduced TBK1-IRF3 complexes in trVLP-infected cells.

claim: Decreased TBK1–IRF3 association was demonstrated by immunoprecipitation.
source: Decreased TBK1–IRF3 association was further demonstrated by immunoprecipitation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3C showing reduced IRF3 co-immunoprecipitation with TBK1 in the presence of EBOV minigenome.

claim: SeV infection-induced IRF3 phosphorylation was significantly inhibited by EBOV trVLPs.
source: Moreover, as shown in Figure 3D, Sendai virus (SeV) infection-induced IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation were significantly inhibited by EBOV trVLPs (Figure 3D and Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting in Figure 3D showing reduced IRF3 phosphorylation at S396 in the presence of EBOV minigenome.

claim: SeV infection-induced IRF3 nuclear translocation was significantly inhibited by EBOV trVLPs.
source: Moreover, as shown in Figure 3D, Sendai virus (SeV) infection-induced IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation were significantly inhibited by EBOV trVLPs (Figure 3D and Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 4A and quantification in Figure 4B showing reduced nuclear IRF3 in trVLP-infected cells.

claim: IRF3 was recruited into IB-like compartments in the cytoplasm in cells infected with live EBOV.
source: Importantly, IRF3 was also recruited into IB-like compartments in the cytoplasm in the cells infected with live EBOV (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 4C showing IRF3 colocalization with NP in live EBOV-infected cells.

claim: The EBOV-mediated sequestration of IRF3 in IBs blocks IRF3 phosphorylation in the TBK1–IRF3 signaling cascade.
source: These data collectively suggested that the EBOV-mediated sequestration of IRF3 in IBs blocks IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation in the TBK1–IRF3 signaling cascade, which is critical for IFN induction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing reduced IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation.

claim: The EBOV-mediated sequestration of IRF3 in IBs blocks IRF3 nuclear translocation in the TBK1–IRF3 signaling cascade.
source: These data collectively suggested that the EBOV-mediated sequestration of IRF3 in IBs blocks IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation in the TBK1–IRF3 signaling cascade, which is critical for IFN induction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing reduced IRF3 nuclear translocation.

claim: The TBK1–IRF3 signaling cascade is critical for IFN induction.
source: These data collectively suggested that the EBOV-mediated sequestration of IRF3 in IBs blocks IRF3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation in the TBK1–IRF3 signaling cascade, which is critical for IFN induction.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the IFN induction pathway.

claim: Ectopic expression of NP alone in cells is sufficient to form IB-like structures.
source: Ectopic expression of NP alone (Noda et al., 2007) or NP and the VP35 protein (Noda et al., 2011) in cells was sufficient to form IB-like structures.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Noda et al., 2007.

claim: Ectopic expression of NP and VP35 in cells is sufficient to form IB-like structures.
source: Ectopic expression of NP alone (Noda et al., 2007) or NP and the VP35 protein (Noda et al., 2011) in cells was sufficient to form IB-like structures.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Noda et al., 2011.

claim: Coexpression of NP and VP35 resulted in substantial sequestration of IRF3 in the IB-like structure.
source: Coexpression of NP and VP35 resulted in substantial sequestration of IRF3 in the IB-like structure, which in turn resulted in a significant reduction of IRF3 in the nucleus, as observed in the cells transfected with vectors only and treated with poly(I:C) (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 5A and quantification in Figure 5B showing IRF3 sequestration in IB-like structures.

claim: Coexpression of NP and VP35 resulted in a significant reduction of IRF3 in the nucleus.
source: Coexpression of NP and VP35 resulted in substantial sequestration of IRF3 in the IB-like structure, which in turn resulted in a significant reduction of IRF3 in the nucleus, as observed in the cells transfected with vectors only and treated with poly(I:C) (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 5A and quantification in Figure 5B showing reduced nuclear IRF3.

claim: Little if any VP35 or NP interacted with IRF3 by immunoprecipitation.
source: Little if any VP35 or NP was demonstrated to interact with IRF3 by immunoprecipitation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B showing no co-immunoprecipitation of IRF3 with VP35 or NP.

claim: The presence of protein L, VP30 and VP24 showed little, if any, effects on IB-like structure formation compared to NP/VP35 coexpression.
source: Compared to NP/VP35 coexpression, the presence of protein L, VP30 and VP24 showed little, if any, effects on IB-like structure formation, IRF3 sequestration and nuclear IRF3 levels (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing similar IB-like structures with or without L, VP30, VP24.

claim: The presence of protein L, VP30 and VP24 showed little, if any, effects on IRF3 sequestration compared to NP/VP35 coexpression.
source: Compared to NP/VP35 coexpression, the presence of protein L, VP30 and VP24 showed little, if any, effects on IB-like structure formation, IRF3 sequestration and nuclear IRF3 levels (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing similar IRF3 sequestration with or without L, VP30, VP24.

claim: The presence of protein L, VP30 and VP24 showed little, if any, effects on nuclear IRF3 levels compared to NP/VP35 coexpression.
source: Compared to NP/VP35 coexpression, the presence of protein L, VP30 and VP24 showed little, if any, effects on IB-like structure formation, IRF3 sequestration and nuclear IRF3 levels (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B showing similar nuclear IRF3 levels with or without L, VP30, VP24.

claim: IB-like structures and VP35 expression are indispensable for IRF3 sequestration.
source: These results suggested that IB-like structures as well as VP35 expression were indispensable for IRF3 sequestration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that NP/VP35 coexpression is necessary and sufficient for IRF3 sequestration.

claim: STING is an endoplasmic reticulum adaptor associated with IRF3.
source: Stimulator of IFN genes (STING), an endoplasmic reticulum adaptor associated with IRF3 (Petrasek et al., 2013), was observed to interact with VP35 (Figure 6A) and be recruited into IBs when the cells were infected by EBOV trVLPs (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petrasek et al., 2013.

claim: STING interacts with VP35.
source: Stimulator of IFN genes (STING), an endoplasmic reticulum adaptor associated with IRF3 (Petrasek et al., 2013), was observed to interact with VP35 (Figure 6A) and be recruited into IBs when the cells were infected by EBOV trVLPs (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A showing co-immunoprecipitation of STING with VP35.

claim: STING is recruited into IBs when cells are infected by EBOV trVLPs.
source: Stimulator of IFN genes (STING), an endoplasmic reticulum adaptor associated with IRF3 (Petrasek et al., 2013), was observed to interact with VP35 (Figure 6A) and be recruited into IBs when the cells were infected by EBOV trVLPs (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 6B, C showing STING colocalization with VP35 in IBs.

claim: A substantial portion of STING was recruited into IBs at 36 hpi in EBOV trVLP-infected cells.
source: A substantial portion of STING was found to be recruited into IBs at 36 hpi in EBOV trVLP-infected cells (Figure 6D, E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 6D, E and quantification in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing STING recruitment to IBs over time.

claim: STING knockdown by siRNA inhibited IRF3 sequestration in viral IBs.
source: STING knockdown by small interfering RNA (siRNA) inhibited IRF3 sequestration in viral IBs (Figure 6F, G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 6F and immunoblotting in Figure 6G showing reduced IRF3 sequestration when STING is knocked down.

claim: STING plays important roles in the sequestration of IRF3 in viral IBs, possibly by interacting with VP35.
source: These results suggested that STING played important roles in the sequestration of IRF3 in viral IBs, possibly by interacting with VP35.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations that STING interacts with VP35, is recruited to IBs, and its knockdown reduces IRF3 sequestration.

claim: Expression of VP35 resulted in a mild inhibition of SeV-induced IFN-β-Luc expression.
source: As reported previously (Basler et al., 2000), expression of VP35 (Figure 7A), but not NP, resulted in a mild inhibition of SeV-induced IFN-β-Luc expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 7A, B showing reduced IFN-β expression with VP35 expression, and is supported by a citation to Basler et al., 2000.

claim: Expression of NP did not result in inhibition of SeV-induced IFN-β-Luc expression.
source: As reported previously (Basler et al., 2000), expression of VP35 (Figure 7A), but not NP, resulted in a mild inhibition of SeV-induced IFN-β-Luc expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 7A showing no significant inhibition with NP expression alone.

claim: Coexpression of VP35 and NP suppressed IFN-β-Luc expression much more potently than VP35 expression alone.
source: Coexpression of VP35 and NP, which led to the formation of IBs and the sequestration of IRF3 (Figure 5A), suppressed IFN-β-Luc expression much more potently than VP35 expression alone (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 7B showing greater suppression with NP/VP35 coexpression compared to VP35 alone.

claim: Coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 was more potent in the inhibition of SeV-induced IFN-β-Luc expression than NP/VP35.
source: Coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 was more potent in the inhibition of SeV-induced IFN-β-Luc expression than NP/VP35 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 7B showing greater suppression with NP/VP35/L/VP30 compared to NP/VP35.

claim: Coexpression of NP/VP35/VP30/L almost completely suppressed poly(I:C)-induced IFN-β transcription.
source: Moreover, coexpression of NP/VP35/VP30/L almost completely suppressed poly(I:C)-induced IFN-β transcription (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7C showing near-complete suppression of IFN-β mRNA with NP/VP35/VP30/L coexpression.

claim: IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on IFN-β transcription upon NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression.
source: IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on IFN-β transcription upon NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which suggested that NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression was similarly powerful as IRF3 depletion in antagonizing IFN-β expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7C showing no further reduction in IFN-β transcription in IRF3-/- cells with NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression.

claim: NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression is similarly powerful as IRF3 depletion in antagonizing IFN-β expression.
source: IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on IFN-β transcription upon NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which suggested that NP/VP35/L/VP30 coexpression was similarly powerful as IRF3 depletion in antagonizing IFN-β expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that IRF3 knockout does not further reduce IFN-β transcription when NP/VP35/L/VP30 are coexpressed.

claim: In wild-type cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 had a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of CXCL10 than VP35 expression alone.
source: In wild-type cells but not IRF3-depleted cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 had a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of IFN-β downstream genes, such as CXCL10, ISG15, and ISG56, than VP35 expression alone (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7D showing greater suppression of CXCL10 mRNA with NP/VP35/L/VP30 compared to VP35 alone in wild-type cells.

claim: In wild-type cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 had a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of ISG15 than VP35 expression alone.
source: In wild-type cells but not IRF3-depleted cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 had a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of IFN-β downstream genes, such as CXCL10, ISG15, and ISG56, than VP35 expression alone (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7E showing greater suppression of ISG15 mRNA with NP/VP35/L/VP30 compared to VP35 alone in wild-type cells.

claim: In wild-type cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 had a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of ISG56 than VP35 expression alone.
source: In wild-type cells but not IRF3-depleted cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 had a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of IFN-β downstream genes, such as CXCL10, ISG15, and ISG56, than VP35 expression alone (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7F showing greater suppression of ISG56 mRNA with NP/VP35/L/VP30 compared to VP35 alone in wild-type cells.

claim: In IRF3-depleted cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 did not have a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of IFN-β downstream genes than VP35 expression alone.
source: In wild-type cells but not IRF3-depleted cells, the coexpression of NP/VP35/L/VP30 had a significantly greater ability to inhibit SeV-induced transcription of IFN-β downstream genes, such as CXCL10, ISG15, and ISG56, than VP35 expression alone (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7D-F showing similar suppression levels in IRF3-/- cells with VP35 alone or NP/VP35/L/VP30.

claim: The sequestration of IRF3 in viral IBs is substantially more powerful than VP35 expression in inhibiting IFN-I production.
source: These results strongly suggested that the sequestration of IRF3 in viral IBs was substantially more powerful than that upon VP35 expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that NP/VP35 coexpression (which forms IBs and sequesters IRF3) is more potent than VP35 alone in suppressing IFN-I production.

claim: Compared with wild-type cells, IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on EBOV trVLPs replication.
source: Compared with wild-type cells, IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on EBOV replication, as indicated by luciferase activity, suggesting that trVLPs efficiently blocked IRF3 signaling (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data in Figure 7G showing similar trVLP replication levels in wild-type and IRF3-/- cells.

claim: trVLPs efficiently blocked IRF3 signaling.
source: Compared with wild-type cells, IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on EBOV replication, as indicated by luciferase activity, suggesting that trVLPs efficiently blocked IRF3 signaling (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that IRF3 knockout does not further enhance trVLP replication.

claim: The overexpression of IRF3/5D, but not IRF3, inhibited EBOV trVLPs replication in IRF3-depleted cells.
source: Moreover, the overexpression of IRF3/5D (a phospho-mimic of activated IRF3), but not IRF3, inhibited EBOV trVLPs replication in IRF3-depleted cells (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data in Figure 7G showing reduced trVLP replication with IRF3/5D but not IRF3 overexpression in IRF3-/- cells.

claim: Compared with wild-type cells, IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on EBOV replication in cells infected with live EBOV.
source: Importantly, compared with wild-type cells, IRF3 depletion showed little, if any, effect on EBOV replication in the cells infected with live EBOV (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by viral titer data in Figure 7H showing similar EBOV replication levels in wild-type and IRF3-/- cells.

claim: The hijacking of IRF3 and sequestration into IBs by EBOV can be significantly more potent in the inhibition of IFN-I production.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the hijacking of IRF3 and sequestration into IBs by EBOV can be significantly more potent in the inhibition of IFN-I production and thereby antagonizes the inhibitory effect of IFN-I on viral replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing enhanced IFN-I suppression with IB formation compared to VP35 alone.

claim: The hijacking of IRF3 and sequestration into IBs by EBOV antagonizes the inhibitory effect of IFN-I on viral replication.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the hijacking of IRF3 and sequestration into IBs by EBOV can be significantly more potent in the inhibition of IFN-I production and thereby antagonizes the inhibitory effect of IFN-I on viral replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that IRF3 sequestration suppresses IFN-I production, which would otherwise inhibit viral replication.

claim: EBOV has established multiple ways to antagonize host innate immune responses to maintain viral replication.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that EBOV has established multiple ways to antagonize host innate immune responses to maintain viral replication.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by accumulated scientific knowledge.

claim: Several EBOV proteins (VP35, VP24, GP, VP30, and VP40) participate in host immune evasion to facilitate viral replication and pathogenesis.
source: Several EBOV proteins (VP35, VP24, GP, VP30, and VP40) are known to participate in host immune evasion to facilitate viral replication and pathogenesis (Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021; Cantoni and Rossman, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021; Cantoni and Rossman, 2018.

claim: VP35 suppresses IFN-I production by inhibiting IRF3/7 phosphorylation.
source: VP35 was demonstrated to suppress IFN-I production by inhibiting IRF3/7 phosphorylation, disrupting DC maturation, and facilitating the escape of immune sensation by dsRNA (Basler, 2015; Cárdenas et al., 2006; Messaoudi et al., 2015; Prins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basler, 2015; Cárdenas et al., 2006; Messaoudi et al., 2015; Prins et al., 2009.

claim: VP35 suppresses IFN-I production by disrupting DC maturation.
source: VP35 was demonstrated to suppress IFN-I production by inhibiting IRF3/7 phosphorylation, disrupting DC maturation, and facilitating the escape of immune sensation by dsRNA (Basler, 2015; Cárdenas et al., 2006; Messaoudi et al., 2015; Prins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basler, 2015; Cárdenas et al., 2006; Messaoudi et al., 2015; Prins et al., 2009.

claim: VP35 suppresses IFN-I production by facilitating the escape of immune sensation by dsRNA.
source: VP35 was demonstrated to suppress IFN-I production by inhibiting IRF3/7 phosphorylation, disrupting DC maturation, and facilitating the escape of immune sensation by dsRNA (Basler, 2015; Cárdenas et al., 2006; Messaoudi et al., 2015; Prins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basler, 2015; Cárdenas et al., 2006; Messaoudi et al., 2015; Prins et al., 2009.

claim: VP30 suppresses RNA silencing by interacting with Dicer.
source: VP30 and VP40 suppress RNA silencing by interacting with Dicer and modulating RNA interference components via exosomes, respectively (Fabozzi et al., 2011; Pleet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fabozzi et al., 2011.

claim: VP40 suppresses RNA silencing by modulating RNA interference components via exosomes.
source: VP30 and VP40 suppress RNA silencing by interacting with Dicer and modulating RNA interference components via exosomes, respectively (Fabozzi et al., 2011; Pleet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pleet et al., 2017.

claim: VP24 blocks IFN-I signaling by hiding type I MHC-1 on the cell surface.
source: VP24 and GP are also known to block IFN-I signaling by hiding type I major histocompatibility complex (MHC-1) on the cell surface and counteracting tetherin or interfering with established immune responses by adsorbing antibodies against GP, respectively (Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021.

claim: GP blocks IFN-I signaling by counteracting tetherin.
source: VP24 and GP are also known to block IFN-I signaling by hiding type I major histocompatibility complex (MHC-1) on the cell surface and counteracting tetherin or interfering with established immune responses by adsorbing antibodies against GP, respectively (Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021.

claim: GP interferes with established immune responses by adsorbing antibodies against GP.
source: VP24 and GP are also known to block IFN-I signaling by hiding type I major histocompatibility complex (MHC-1) on the cell surface and counteracting tetherin or interfering with established immune responses by adsorbing antibodies against GP, respectively (Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Audet and Kobinger, 2015; Bhattacharyya, 2021.

claim: Viral IBs are a characteristic of cellular EBOV infection.
source: Viral IBs are a characteristic of cellular EBOV infection and are important sites for viral RNA replication, and NP and VP35 are extremely critical proteins for the formation of IBs (Hoenen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoenen et al., 2012.

claim: Viral IBs are important sites for viral RNA replication.
source: Viral IBs are a characteristic of cellular EBOV infection and are important sites for viral RNA replication, and NP and VP35 are extremely critical proteins for the formation of IBs (Hoenen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoenen et al., 2012.

claim: NP and VP35 are extremely critical proteins for the formation of IBs.
source: Viral IBs are a characteristic of cellular EBOV infection and are important sites for viral RNA replication, and NP and VP35 are extremely critical proteins for the formation of IBs (Hoenen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoenen et al., 2012.

claim: Whether viral IBs are involved in antagonizing IFN-I production during EBOV trVLPs infection has not yet been reported.
source: However, whether viral IBs are involved in antagonizing IFN-I production during EBOV trVLPs infection has not yet been reported.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: IRF3 is hijacked and sequestered into EBOV IBs by viral infection.
source: Here, we found that IRF3 is hijacked and sequestered into EBOV IBs by viral infection (Figure 1A), which demonstrates that viral IBs are utilized for IRF3 compartmentalization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 1A showing IRF3 colocalization with VP35 in IBs.

claim: Viral IBs are utilized for IRF3 compartmentalization.
source: Here, we found that IRF3 is hijacked and sequestered into EBOV IBs by viral infection (Figure 1A), which demonstrates that viral IBs are utilized for IRF3 compartmentalization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that IRF3 is sequestered in IBs.

claim: The compartmentalization of IRF3 in IBs resulted in the spatial isolation of IRF3 from the kinases TBK1 and IKKε.
source: Meanwhile, this compartmentalization resulted in the spatial isolation of IRF3 from the kinases TBK1 and IKKε (Figure 1C, E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 1C, E showing no colocalization of TBK1 or IKKε with IBs.

claim: IRF3 deprivation by viral IBs may antagonize host antiviral signaling by inhibiting IFN-I production signaling.
source: This suggests that IRF3 deprivation by viral IBs may antagonize host antiviral signaling by inhibiting IFN-I production signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that IRF3 is sequestered away from its activators.

claim: The expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L was significantly more antagonistic to SeV-induced IFN-β production than the expression of VP35 alone.
source: As expected, the expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L, which is involved in the composition of IBs, was significantly more antagonistic to SeV-induced IFN-β production than the expression of VP35 alone (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 7B showing greater suppression with NP/VP35/VP30/L compared to VP35 alone.

claim: The expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L can significantly antagonize the promoting effect of poly(I:C) on IFN-β transcription.
source: In addition, the expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L can significantly antagonize the promoting effect of poly(I:C) on IFN-β transcription, and IRF3 knockout could not further inhibit the transcription of IFN-β (Figure 7C), which may be because viral hijacking of IRF3 into IBs nearly completely antagonized its function of promoting IFN-β production.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7C showing suppression of poly(I:C)-induced IFN-β transcription with NP/VP35/VP30/L expression.

claim: Viral hijacking of IRF3 into IBs nearly completely antagonized its function of promoting IFN-β production.
source: In addition, the expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L can significantly antagonize the promoting effect of poly(I:C) on IFN-β transcription, and IRF3 knockout could not further inhibit the transcription of IFN-β (Figure 7C), which may be because viral hijacking of IRF3 into IBs nearly completely antagonized its function of promoting IFN-β production.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that IRF3 knockout does not further reduce IFN-β transcription when NP/VP35/VP30/L are expressed.

claim: The effect of poly(I:C) is consistent with the results obtained with SeV, which indicates that poly(I:C) may mainly activate the RLR signaling pathway.
source: In this study, the effect of poly(I:C) is consistent with the results obtained with SeV, which indicates that poly(I:C) may mainly activate the RLR signaling pathway (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that poly(I:C) and SeV produce similar effects on IFN-β production.

claim: The expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L significantly inhibited the ability of SeV to promote the transcription of IFN-β downstream genes (CXCL10, ISG15, and ISG56) but did not completely suppress the effect of SeV.
source: As shown in Figure 7D–F, the expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L significantly inhibited the ability of SeV to promote the transcription of IFN-β downstream genes (CXCL10, ISG15, and ISG56) but did not completely suppress the effect of SeV, which may be due to the low transfection rate of HeLa cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7D-F showing partial suppression of downstream gene transcription.

claim: The incomplete suppression of SeV-induced downstream gene transcription by NP/VP35/VP30/L may be due to the low transfection rate of HeLa cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7D–F, the expression of NP/VP35/VP30/L significantly inhibited the ability of SeV to promote the transcription of IFN-β downstream genes (CXCL10, ISG15, and ISG56) but did not completely suppress the effect of SeV, which may be due to the low transfection rate of HeLa cells.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the incomplete suppression observed.

claim: The knockout of IRF3 in cells could not further promote EBOV and EBOV trVLPs replication compared with that observed in wild-type cells.
source: Furthermore, the knockout of IRF3 in cells could not further promote EBOV and EBOV trVLPs replication compared with that observed in wild-type cells (Figure 7G, H), which may have been because IRF3 was hijacked into viral IBs and could not be phosphorylated into the nucleus to regulate IFN-I production.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data in Figure 7G and viral titer data in Figure 7H showing no difference in replication between wild-type and IRF3-/- cells.

claim: IRF3 was hijacked into viral IBs and could not be phosphorylated into the nucleus to regulate IFN-I production.
source: Furthermore, the knockout of IRF3 in cells could not further promote EBOV and EBOV trVLPs replication compared with that observed in wild-type cells (Figure 7G, H), which may have been because IRF3 was hijacked into viral IBs and could not be phosphorylated into the nucleus to regulate IFN-I production.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain why IRF3 knockout does not enhance viral replication.

claim: Viral IBs act as virus-built 'jails' to imprison transcription factors.
source: These results suggest that viral IBs act as virus-built 'jails' to imprison transcription factors and present a novel and possible common mechanism of viral immune evasion in which the critical signaling molecule IRF3 is spatially segregated from the antiviral kinases TBK1 and IKKε.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing IRF3 sequestration in IBs.

claim: EBOV presents a novel and possible common mechanism of viral immune evasion in which IRF3 is spatially segregated from TBK1 and IKKε.
source: These results suggest that viral IBs act as virus-built 'jails' to imprison transcription factors and present a novel and possible common mechanism of viral immune evasion in which the critical signaling molecule IRF3 is spatially segregated from the antiviral kinases TBK1 and IKKε.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing IRF3 sequestration in IBs away from TBK1 and IKKε.

claim: Neither VP35 nor NP interacted with IRF3.
source: Although almost all IRF3 could be sequestered to viral IBs formed by VP35 and NP (Figure 5A, B), we found that neither VP35 nor NP interacted with IRF3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing no co-immunoprecipitation of IRF3 with VP35 or NP.

claim: VP35 interacts with STING and colocalizes in IBs.
source: Here, we found that VP35 interacts with STING and colocalizes in IBs and that knockdown of STING inhibits the sequestration of IRF3 in IBs (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A and immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 6B-E showing VP35-STING interaction and colocalization.

claim: Knockdown of STING inhibits the sequestration of IRF3 in IBs.
source: Here, we found that VP35 interacts with STING and colocalizes in IBs and that knockdown of STING inhibits the sequestration of IRF3 in IBs (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 6F and immunoblotting in Figure 6G showing reduced IRF3 sequestration with STING knockdown.

claim: VP35 may hijack IRF3 into IBs through STING.
source: These results suggest that VP35 may hijack IRF3 into IBs through STING.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations that VP35 interacts with STING, STING is in IBs, and STING knockdown reduces IRF3 sequestration.

claim: Whether other host proteins are involved in IRF3 sequestration and the role of NP in the recruitment of IRF3 by VP35 remain unclear.
source: However, whether other host proteins are involved in this process and the role of NP in the recruitment of IRF3 by VP35 remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: Whether VP35 activates the STING-IRF3 pathway in a cGAS-independent manner by interacting with STING and the molecular mechanism remain to be further investigated.
source: In addition, we found that VP35 may hijack IRF3 into IBs via STING association (Figure 6A–C); however, whether VP35 activates the STING-IRF3 pathway in a cGAS-independent manner by interacting with STING and the molecular mechanism remain to be further investigated.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: EBOV VP35 sequesters IRF3 into viral IBs and inhibits the association of IRF3 with TBK1 and IKKε, preventing IRF3 from entering the nucleus and thereby inhibiting IFN-I production.
source: In summary, EBOV VP35 sequesters IRF3 into viral IBs and inhibits the association of IRF3 with TBK1 and IKKε, preventing IRF3 from entering the nucleus and thereby inhibiting IFN-I production (Figure 8).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarized in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: This study reveals a new strategy by which EBOV escapes the innate immune response.
source: Therefore, this study reveals a new strategy by which EBOV escapes the innate immune response and provides new ideas for EBOV disease treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: This study provides new ideas for EBOV disease treatment.
source: Therefore, this study reveals a new strategy by which EBOV escapes the innate immune response and provides new ideas for EBOV disease treatment.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential implications of the findings.
